Forth
FORTH
adv.
Old English forth, forð: forward, onward, out from confinement into the open. Webster 1828: forward in time; out; into public view. The KJV uses it of creation bringing forth, of the Word going forth, of Lazarus coming forth, of Israel brought forth from Egypt, and of the church going forth unto Christ without the camp.

Biblical Definition

Forth is the Bible’s small word for a real going-out. God does not leave His works folded in. In the beginning He said, Let the earth bring forth (Gen 1:11), and the earth did. His Word is not a private impression: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void (Isa 55:11). The blessed man bringeth forth his fruit in his season (Ps 1:3). Redemption is a bringing-forth: Moses is sent that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt (Ex 3:10). Resurrection is a coming-forth: Jesus cried, Lazarus, come forth (John 11:43), and the dead man came. Discipleship is a going-forth: Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach (Heb 13:13). The adverb therefore traces a single pattern: what God has spoken, planted, redeemed, or raised does not stay inside. It comes out — fruit, people, Word, the living man, the church following a crucified Lord outside the gate. The opposite of forth in this register is not rest; it is the refusal to be sent, the Word left unspoken, the fruit unborne, the camp that will not bear reproach.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FORTH as forward, onward in time; out; aboard; noting progression from confinement; out into public view or public character.

expand to see more

FORTH, adv. — Forward; onward in time; in advance; as from that day forth; from that time forth.

FORTH, adv. — Out; aboard; noting progression or advance from a state of confinement; as, the plants in spring put forth leaves.

FORTH, adv. — Out into public view, or public character. Your country calls you forth into its service.

FORTH, prep. — Out of. (Little used in this construction in modern English; the KJV’s ordinary use is adverbial.)

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:11 — "And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so."

Isaiah 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

John 11:43 — "And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth."

Exodus 3:10 — "Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt."

Hebrews 13:13 — "Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach."

Modern Corruption

Forth is corrupted when going-out is recast as self-expression (“put yourself out there,” “speak your truth”), when the Word that goes forth is treated as inner voice rather than God’s mouth, and when the church refuses to go forth without the camp because reproach is bad branding.

expand to see more

Therapeutic and expressive-individualist English has stolen the motion of forth and aimed it at the self. “Put yourself out there.” “Speak your truth.” “Come out” as an identity liturgy. Scripture’s going-forth is not the self arriving on a stage. It is God’s Word leaving His mouth and doing what He sent it to do; it is a people brought out of bondage by His hand; it is a dead man obeying Christ’s cry; it is the church following Jesus outside the gate. The recovery is to restore the subject: God sends; the earth yields; the Word accomplishes; Lazarus comes because He called.

The ecclesiastical form of the corruption is a church that will not go forth without the camp. Hebrews 13 locates Jesus outside the gate, in reproach, and commands the saints to go to Him there. Seeker-sensitive and platform-evangelical instincts reverse the motion: keep the camp comfortable, keep the brand inside the gate, treat reproach as a marketing failure. The apostolic pattern is the opposite. The gospel is preached in all the world (Mark 16:15); the Word goes forth and does not return void; the disciple follows the Lord outside.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English forth / forð, forward and out. Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Hebrew yātsā’ (H3318) at Isa 55:11; Hebrew nāthan (H5414) at Ps 1:3; Greek exō (G1854) at John 11:43 and Heb 13:13; Greek exerchomai (G1831) at Heb 13:13. Genesis 1:11 and Exodus 3:10 are untagged in this cache; no Hebrew number is invented for them.

expand to see more

Hebrew yātsā’ (H3318) — to go out, go forth (Isa 55:11, goeth forth out of my mouth).

Hebrew nāthan (H5414) — to give, put, bring forth (Ps 1:3, bringeth forth his fruit).

Greek exō (G1854) — out, forth, without (John 11:43, come forth; Heb 13:13, without the camp).

Greek exerchomai (G1831) — to go out, go forth (Heb 13:13, Let us go forth).

Old English forth — forward, out from confinement into the open.

Usage

"Creation, fruit, Word, exodus, resurrection, and discipleship all go forth — God does not leave His works folded in."

"Lazarus, come forth is command, not therapy; the dead man comes because Christ called."

"Hebrews 13:13 locates the Christian life outside the camp with a reproached Lord, not inside a comfortable brand."
